textbookText: From the above graphs, both pressures P and volume V of a gas are the function of a quantity (273.15 + ). The quantity (273.15 + ) is called absolute temperature. The zero value of this scale is called absolute zero temperature. Hence at absolute zero temperature,  + 273.15= T or,  +273.15 = 0   = –273.15°C Therefore, the absolute zero temperature is -273.15C. The extrapolation of P-T and V-T graph shows that the straight lines cut the temperature axis at a point, which is 273.15 divisions below the origin of the degree Celsius scale, in both cases. The temperature value of that point is taken as absolute zero temperature. Hence absolute zero temperature is that temperature at which the pressure of the given mass of a gas becomes zero at a constant volume or the volume of the given mass of a gas becomes zero at a constant pressure.

Significance of absolute zero temperature At absolute zero temperature, the molecular motion stops, and there is no collision between gas molecules. So, all the molecules of a gas are at complete rest at the absolute zero temperature. Also, at the absolute zero temperature, matters are highly condensed. From the above P-T and V-T graphs, if we go beyond -273.15C in the temperature axis, then, the volume of a gas at a constant pressure, and the pressure of a gas at a constant volume becomes negative which is practically impossible. Therefore, negative temperature is impossible in absolute scale or Kelvin scale. 13.4 Ideal Gas Ideal gases are those having zero intermolecular force of attraction. Ideal gases strictly follow Boyle's law and Charles' law. Ideal gas is an ideal concept. Practically, we cannot get an ideal gas. That means each real gas deviates from the ideal gas behavior. However, at a high Physics, Grade 11 | 291

temperature and a low pressure, properties of a real gas are almost similar to those of an ideal gas. For an ideal gas, the intermolecular force of attraction must be zero, but it appears significantly in the case of a real gas.

Ideal Gas Equation When a certain mass of a gas changes from one equilibrium state to another equilibrium state, its pressure, volume and temperature set up a relation between two equilibrium states on the basis of Boyle's law and Charles' law. Hence, the ideal gas equation or equation of state is the interrelationship between pressure, volume and temperature of the given mass of an ideal gas on the basis of Charles’s law and Boyle’s law.
